You are a code worker editing the freytag-forge repo. Your cwd IS a git worktree of /home/bcorfman/dev/freytag-forge. Edit/create files ONLY under the cwd; never edit /home/bcorfman/dev/freytag-forge directly (you may run its .venv/bin/python). Do NOT git commit, do NOT git add -A, do NOT touch .git, do NOT edit anything under storygame/ or data/. OWNED FILES: scripts/disclosure_matrix.py (new), tests/test_disclosure_matrix.py (new), .plans/disclosure-matrix.json (generated), .plans/disclosure-matrix.md (generated). Notes to /home/bcorfman/dev/ringer-work/design-review-step3-notes/notes.md.

GOAL (design review Step 3, 'disclosure vocabulary review', data only): produce a reviewable inventory and a nine-scene matrix of how the narration-safety guards treat every guarded word, so a human can later classify each as public or secret-with-unlock-fact. No engine change. This is Finding 1 of the review: ordinary words must not be blocked as secrets just because they appear in the world model.

READ FIRST: storygame/runtime/narration_safety.py (NarrationSafetyValidator._validate_segments: the guard kinds and their error codes), storygame/story_package/loader.py (_compile_knowledge_indexes: alias_to_knowledge, term_to_knowledge, leak_term_to_knowledge, audience_to_known_terms; and how entity-name scoping/scoped aliases are built), storygame/runtime/knowledge.py, tests/test_design_review_fixtures.py (how to build real engine state for a scene, helper for late-scene state with earned knowledge, how narration is submitted through the validator with a stub provider), tests/test_narration_corpus.py, tests/test_leak_terms.py, tests/test_narration_term_traps.py, data/stories/*/{world.yaml,knowledge.yaml,pacing.yaml}.

BUILD scripts/disclosure_matrix.py (run: PYTHONPATH=$PWD /home/bcorfman/dev/freytag-forge/.venv/bin/python scripts/disclosure_matrix.py [--out-dir .plans]); deterministic, no network, no env vars, sorted output, stable across runs:
1. INVENTORY: for the continuity_initiative package list every guarded term with: term (normalized form), guard kind among exactly these: entity_name (place/NPC/item name or alias from world.yaml), identifier_fragment (a word derived from an identifier such as a scene/phase/fact id, e.g. 'phase' from phase_two), leak_term (declared leak_terms of a knowledge item), knowledge_alias, must_convey_phrase, scoped_alias (aliases scoped to a scene/owner); the owner ids (entity ids / knowledge ids); the scenes in which the owner is available; the unlock fact ids (the establishes facts of the owning knowledge items, if any, and the requires predicates); and a `suggested_class`: 'secret_with_unlock_fact' when the owner is knowledge with an unlock fact and the term is not also an ordinary scene entity name, 'public_candidate' when the term is an ordinary entity name or common word that appears in scene entry text/world descriptions of its available scenes, otherwise 'needs_review'. Say in a `why` string which rule produced the suggestion. Find the real code paths that decide guarding; do not reimplement them loosely: call the loader's index structures and the validator's own helper methods where they exist, and read the validator source to enumerate kinds you cannot get from an index.
2. MATRIX: for each of the nine scenes (1A..3C) and each guarded term whose owner can ever appear in that scene or is guarded in that scene, evaluate three real-engine states and record accepted/rejected plus the exact error code: 'early' (state at scene entry: entry facts of this and all earlier scenes asserted, NO reveal of this scene earned), 'earned' (same plus the establishes facts of the term's owning reveal asserted), 'skipped' (a later-scene state where one earlier reveal owning the term was deliberately not earned, as in tests/test_design_review_fixtures.py's skipped-reveal fixture). Evaluation: build the real state, submit a short neutral narration sentence containing only that term (for example 'The <term> is here.' choose wording that does not contain other guarded terms) through the real narration validator exactly as the fixtures do, catch ProposalValidationError and record its code. Reuse helper construction patterns from the fixtures; copy the minimum into the script rather than importing from tests. Keep total runtime under 60 s (cache states per scene; deep-copy per term).
3. OUTPUT .plans/disclosure-matrix.json (inventory list + matrix rows {scene, term, guard_kind, early, earned, skipped}) and .plans/disclosure-matrix.md: a short human summary with counts per guard kind and per suggested_class, a table of terms whose verdict is 'rejected' in 'earned' (a guard that never releases: likely a bug or a permanent secret), a table of terms 'rejected' in 'early' whose suggested_class is public_candidate (the over-blocking Finding 1 is about), and a table of terms 'accepted' in 'early' whose suggested_class is secret_with_unlock_fact (a possible leak). Do not draw conclusions beyond the data. No term lists copied from your head: everything comes from the package.
4. tests/test_disclosure_matrix.py: hermetic, under 20 s: the script runs and is deterministic (two runs produce identical JSON), every guard kind named above that exists in the package has at least one inventory row (assert the kinds actually present; say in notes which kinds are absent), every matrix cell has a verdict, the three summary tables are consistent with the JSON, and the generated files in .plans match a fresh run (freshness check).
Hard rules: no story-specific names in the script's logic (read all names from the package; the story id is a CLI default only); ruff-clean; match repo style.

HOW TO RUN: confirm `PYTHONPATH=$PWD /home/bcorfman/dev/freytag-forge/.venv/bin/python -c "import storygame; print(storygame.__file__)"` is inside cwd. Run the script, then PYTHONPATH=$PWD TMPDIR=/tmp /home/bcorfman/dev/freytag-forge/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/test_disclosure_matrix.py ; ruff: PYTHONPATH=$PWD /home/bcorfman/dev/freytag-forge/.venv/bin/python -m ruff check --fix . ; -m ruff format . . Reply with files changed and the three table sizes.
